t: How to connect Python database adapters
x: How to connect Python database adapters Use these adapters when a database already exposes Arrow results in Python, is available through SQLAlchemy, or has an ODBC driver. They share the same paths and fsspec operations as the native Rust SQL backends. Connect DuckDB Install the DuckDB extra: python -m pip install 'fsspec-db[duckdb]' Open a database file: import fsspec fs = fsspec.filesystem("db+duckdb", database="warehouse.duckdb") print(fs.ls("/main", detail=False)) orders = fs.query("SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT ?", [100]) To reuse an existing connection, construct the class directly: import duckdb from fsspec_db import DuckDBDatabaseFileSystem connection = duckdb.connect("warehouse.duckdb") fs = DuckDBDatabaseFileSystem(connection=connection) Connect through SQLAlchemy Install SQLAlchemy and the driver for the target database: python -m pip install fsspec-db sqlalchemy Pass a SQLAlchemy URL through the registered protocol: import fsspec fs = fsspec.filesystem("db+sqlalchemy", url="sqlite:///warehouse.db") print(fs.ls("/main", detail=False)) Reuse an engine when the application already owns connection pooling: from sqlalchemy import create_engine from fsspec_db import SQLAlchemyDa

SQLite values are converted into Arrow arrays with a small affinity mapper. Query results use declared column metadata plus observed non-null runtime value types, so NULL-first and mixed numeric expression columns can still produce numeric Arrow arrays. SQLite value/type Arrow type boolean-like bool integer-like int64 real/float/double float64 blob/binary binary everything else utf8 For writes, Arrow Null columns bind SQLite NULL. Temporal arrays are bound as integer epoch values. When a query produces mixed SQLite runtime types in one expression column, cast explicitly in SQL for predictable Arrow output.

The sqlx backends convert common database scalar types into Arrow: Backend Database type family Arrow type PostgreSQL BOOL bool PostgreSQL INT2, INT4, INT8, OID int64 PostgreSQL FLOAT4, FLOAT8 float64 PostgreSQL BYTEA binary PostgreSQL TEXT, VARCHAR, CHAR, BPCHAR utf8 MySQL BOOLEAN bool MySQL signed and unsigned integer families int64 MySQL FLOAT, DOUBLE float64 MySQL BINARY, VARBINARY, *BLOB binary MySQL CHAR, VARCHAR, *TEXT, JSON, enums utf8 Additional native output mappings are: Backend Database type Arrow type PostgreSQL DATE date32 PostgreSQL TIME time64[us] PostgreSQL TIMESTAMP, TIMESTAMPTZ timestamp[us] without timezone metadata PostgreSQL NUMERIC, UUID, JSON, JSONB utf8 containing the decoded value’s text representation MySQL DATE date32 MySQL DATETIME, TIMESTAMP timestamp[us] without timezone metadata MySQL DECIMAL, JSON utf8 containing the decoded value’s text representation PostgreSQL NAME also maps to UTF-8. MySQL YEAR and BIT follow the integer mapping; SET follows the string mapping. Unsigned MySQL integers that do not fit in Arrow int64 return an error. Non-null output types absent from these mappings raise an unsupported-type error; explicit SQL casts can select a s

SQLite introspection uses PRAGMA database_list, sqlite_master, table_info, index_list, index_info, and foreign_key_list. Schema listings do not count every relation; relation lookups inspect the requested relation. PostgreSQL uses information_schema and pg_catalog. Root listings exclude pg_catalog, information_schema, and toast schemas. MySQL uses information_schema and excludes information_schema, mysql, performance_schema, and sys from root listings. MySQL database names are schema directories. Native PostgreSQL overwrite uses TRUNCATE TABLE; MySQL and SQLite use DELETE FROM in the insertion transaction. Python adapter atomicity depends on the adapter. ODBC lists no indexes and does not provide portable view definitions. Native queries expose RecordBatchStream through the Rust Database trait. The current sqlx backends construct Arrow arrays from rows. ArrowExtraction records the extraction strategy without changing path semantics.

t: Why database objects have filesystem paths
x: Why database objects have filesystem paths fsspec tools expect directory listings, metadata, and file-like reads. Mapping SQL objects to those operations lets a browser or data consumer use a database through an interface it already understands. Relations have structure and data A table or view is directory-like because it contains metadata facets: columns, indexes, constraints, and view dependencies. Rows are separate virtual files, selected by an extension on the relation path. This avoids confusing a table’s structure with a particular encoding of its data. Those files are generated representations rather than stored database objects. Reading Parquet runs a query and encodes its result. A reported byte size may be unknown until encoding completes. A small byte read is therefore not necessarily a cheap database query. One mapping supports several database implementations The Rust Database trait owns database primitives. DatabaseFs turns them into filesystem behavior: parsing paths, generating SQL, and encoding data. Python classes inherit from AbstractFileSystem and delegate those primitives through PyO3, retaining fsspec’s surrounding interface. Native SQL backends use sqlx. Pyt

t: Why database objects have filesystem paths
s: One mapping supports several database implementations
x: The Rust Database trait owns database primitives. DatabaseFs turns them into filesystem behavior: parsing paths, generating SQL, and encoding data. Python classes inherit from AbstractFileSystem and delegate those primitives through PyO3, retaining fsspec’s surrounding interface. Native SQL backends use sqlx. Python adapters implement AbstractDatabase. They can use the reverse bridge or the direct PyDatabaseFileSystem implementation of the same path model. Metadata depth and type fidelity still depend on the underlying database and adapter.

t: Why database objects have filesystem paths
s: SQL and path reads serve different needs
x: A relation path expresses a bounded selection from one relation. A SQL query can express joins, aggregations, or database-specific operations. Both return Arrow data, but a common representation does not make every database type portable. Explicit SQL casts can make type conversion predictable across backends.

t: Why database objects have filesystem paths
s: Writes and transactions cross another boundary
x: Writing a data file decodes rows and inserts them into an existing relation. Overwrite replaces rows; append retains them. Guarded filesystem DDL methods create, rename, or remove relations separately. A native write handle commits on successful close and discards on an exceptional context exit. Deferred fsspec transactions postpone each file commit, but they do not make several independent file commits one atomic database transaction. Adapter transaction behavior can also differ from native backends. See Paths and metadata for the namespace and How to manage tables and metadata caches for mutation tasks.

t: How to manage tables and metadata caches
x: How to manage tables and metadata caches Enable DDL when an application needs filesystem mutation methods. These examples create and remove a table in managed.db. Create and rename a table import fsspec import pyarrow as pa fs = fsspec.filesystem("db+sqlite", database="managed.db", allow_ddl=True) fs.mkdir("/main/events", schema=pa.schema([pa.field("id", pa.int64())])) fs.mv("/main/events", "/main/archived_events") print(fs.ls("/main", detail=False)) The listing contains /main/archived_events. Use sql="CREATE TABLE ..." instead of schema= when database-specific types or constraints are needed. The flag guards filesystem DDL helpers; raw query() retains normal SQL permissions. Refresh external changes Bypass stale introspection after another connection changes database objects: fs.ls("/main", detail=False, refresh=True) fs.info("/main/archived_events", refresh=True) Set listings_expiry_time and max_paths at construction to bound cache lifetime and entries. Call fs.invalidate_cache() to clear introspection explicitly. Defer writes until a transaction exits Encode rows and group deferred writes with fsspec’s transaction context: import pyarrow.ipc as ipc rows = pa.table({"id": [1, 2]}

t: How to manage tables and metadata caches
s: Defer writes until a transaction exits
x: Encode rows and group deferred writes with fsspec’s transaction context: import pyarrow.ipc as ipc rows = pa.table({"id": [1, 2]}) sink = pa.BufferOutputStream() with ipc.new_stream(sink, rows.schema) as writer: writer.write_table(rows) with fs.transaction: with fs.open("/main/archived_events.arrow", "ab") as file: file.write(sink.getvalue().to_pybytes()) print(fs.query("SELECT id FROM archived_events ORDER BY id").to_pylist()) The result is [{'id': 1}, {'id': 2}]. Exceptions before transaction completion discard deferred buffers. Each file commits separately; use a backend’s database transaction API when several writes must be atomic together.

Path Meaning / Root, listing schemas/catalogs. /{schema} Schema directory, listing tables and views. /{schema}/{relation} Relation directory, listing metadata facets. /{schema}/{relation}/columns Column facet directory. /{schema}/{relation}/columns/{column} Column metadata item. /{schema}/{relation}/indexes Index facet directory. /{schema}/{relation}/indexes/{index} Index metadata item. /{schema}/{relation}/constraints Constraint facet directory. /{schema}/{relation}/constraints/{constraint} Constraint metadata item. /{schema}/{view}/depends_on View dependency facet directory. /{schema}/{view}/depends_on/{relation} A relation the view reads, with target. /{schema}/{view}/definition.sql View definition SQL. /{schema}/{relation}.arrow Materialized relation as Arrow IPC stream. /{schema}/{relation}.parquet Materialized relation as Parquet. /{schema}/{relation}.csv Materialized relation as CSV. /{schema}/{relation}.jsonl Materialized relation as line-delimited JSON. /{schema}/{relation}.sql Relation DDL text. SQLite normally exposes the default database as /main. Native backends render relation .sql data paths. The direct PyDatabaseFileSystem adapter raises NotImplementedError for rela

fs.ls("/", detail=False) # ["/main"] fs.ls("/main", detail=False) # ["/main/users", "/main/active_users"] fs.ls("/main/users", detail=False) # ["/main/users/columns", "/main/users/indexes", "/main/users/constraints"] detail=True returns fsspec info dictionaries: fs.ls("/main/users/columns", detail=True)

fs.info("/main/users") fs.info("/main/users/columns/id") fs.info("/main/users/indexes/idx_users_name") Relation info includes kind and may include row_count. Column info includes database type, nullability, ordinal position, and primary-key status.

Four query parameters are available on materialized relation paths: Parameter Example Status columns /main/users.arrow?columns=id,name Selects a column list. limit /main/users.parquet?limit=100 Adds LIMIT. offset /main/users.arrow?limit=20&offset=20 Skips rows before applying the limit. where /main/users.arrow?where=score > 10 Adds a WHERE predicate (see below). Query values are URL-decoded, so percent-encoded predicates such as ?where=score%20%3E%2010 are equivalent to the unencoded form. data = fs.cat_file("/main/users.arrow?columns=id,name&limit=10&where=id > 0")

The where value is parsed as a single boolean SQL expression with a dialect-aware parser, re-serialized from its AST, and appended as a WHERE clause. Because only a parsed expression is ever emitted, multi-statement or non-expression payloads are rejected with a ValueError rather than interpolated: fs.cat_file("/main/users.arrow?where=score > 10") # ok fs.cat_file("/main/users.arrow?where=1); DROP TABLE x;--") # rejected fs.query() accepts arbitrary SQL beyond a single predicate.

Data writes use the same materialized relation paths as reads: with fs.open("/main/users.arrow", "ab") as f: f.write(arrow_ipc_bytes) The incoming file extension controls decoding. .arrow and .parquet carry their own schema. .csv and .jsonl are decoded using the database table schema.

info() and ls(detail=True) return ordinary fsspec dictionaries with these common keys: Key Meaning name Absolute fsspec-db path, without protocol. type "directory" for schemas, relations, and facets; "file" for metadata items and materialized data. size Byte size when known. Materialized table reads usually learn size only after encoding. kind fsspec-db object kind, such as schema, table, view, column, index, or constraint. Extra metadata is stored directly in the same dictionary: Path Extra fields Relation directory kind, optional row_count, optional size_bytes. Column item data_type, nullable, ordinal, primary_key, optional default. Index item columns, unique, optional method. Constraint item kind, columns, optional references, optional expr. Data file format, dialect, size_known.
/{schema}/{relation}/columns/{column} is both a metadata item for info() and a JSON array of distinct, sorted values for reads. limit and offset bound column-value reads; the default limit is 100.

Operation Behavior open(path, "wb") Replaces relation rows when the write commits. open(path, "ab") Appends rows when the write commits. pipe_file(path, bytes) / put_file(local, path) Overwrites by default. pipe_file(..., mode="append") / put_file(..., mode="append") Appends. pipe_file(..., mode="create") / put_file(..., mode="create") Raises FileExistsError for an existing target; does not create a table. Supported open modes are r, rb, w, wb, a, and ab. Exclusive-create and update modes raise NotImplementedError. Writes decode the completed encoded stream at commit time. Unclosed native write handles are discarded.

allow_ddl=False is the default. Guarded mkdir, rm_file, and mv raise PermissionError unless enabled. Raw query() is not restricted by that flag. With DDL enabled, mkdir("/schema/relation", schema=arrow_schema) creates a table; sql= accepts explicit creation SQL. rm_file("/schema/relation") drops the relation, while a relation path with an extension deletes its rows. mv renames relations within one schema; cross-schema moves raise NotImplementedError. ls(..., refresh=True) and info(..., refresh=True) bypass cached introspection. invalidate_cache(path=None) clears all Python and available Rust introspection cache entries, even when a path is supplied. Listing cache options include use_listings_cache, listings_expiry_time, and max_paths.

Python backend contract Python-defined database backends implement fsspec_db.AbstractDatabase. An AbstractDatabaseFileSystem wraps the object and delegates filesystem behavior through the Rust DatabaseFs bridge. Contract AbstractDatabase mirrors the Rust Database trait method set, except for Rust-only default methods such as arrow_extraction. The object must be safe to call from the bridge while the Python GIL is held. Backends return the metadata classes exported by fsspec_db. Class Constructor SchemaInfo SchemaInfo(name, catalog=None, comment=None) RelationInfo RelationInfo(name, kind, row_count=None, size_bytes=None, comment=None) ColumnInfo ColumnInfo(name, data_type, nullable, default, ordinal, primary_key=False, comment=None) IndexInfo IndexInfo(name, columns, unique, method=None) ConstraintInfo ConstraintInfo(name, kind, columns, references=None, expr=None) RelationInfo.kind is table or view. ConstraintInfo.kind is pk, fk, unique, or check.

query(sql, params=None) returns a pyarrow.Table. params contains values representable by the bridge scalar type set: None, bool, int, float, str, and bytes. AbstractDatabaseFileSystem.query() and open_query() call the backend’s query() through the Rust bridge. Path reads such as /main/users.arrow?columns=id&limit=10 generate SQL in Rust and then call the same backend method.

insert(schema, relation, table, mode="append") receives a pyarrow.Table decoded from a relation data file. mode values are: Mode Semantics append Add rows to the existing relation. truncate Replace relation rows before inserting table. The method returns the number of inserted rows.

The bridge maps common Python exceptions to fsspec/Rust error categories. Python exception Meaning FileNotFoundError Missing schema, relation, or item. PermissionError Permission-denied operation. FileExistsError Existing item for create semantics. NotADirectoryError Directory operation on a file. IsADirectoryError File operation on a directory. ValueError Invalid argument or unsupported value. Other exceptions Generic backend error.

AbstractDatabaseFileSystem(db, **storage_options) and PyDatabaseFileSystem(db, **storage_options) adapt a concrete AbstractDatabase. AbstractDatabaseFileSystem routes paths through Rust DatabaseFs. PyDatabaseFileSystem implements the path mapping directly in Python and does not call the Rust bridge. The backend must execute SQL generated for path projection, predicates, limits, and offsets, as well as SQL supplied directly to query. Returning an unchanged in-memory table for every query does not satisfy that contract. Metadata must describe actual relation state. Insert behavior, rollback, and connection lifetime remain backend responsibilities. Existing implementations in fsspec_db.duckdb, fsspec_db.sqlalchemy, and fsspec_db.odbc are concrete adapters.

t: How to connect PostgreSQL or MySQL
x: How to connect PostgreSQL or MySQL PostgreSQL and MySQL are native Rust backends implemented with sqlx. They use the same filesystem path model as SQLite and are exposed as db+postgresql, db+postgres, and db+mysql. Construction import fsspec pg = fsspec.filesystem( "db+postgresql", dsn="postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/app", ) mysql = fsspec.filesystem( "db+mysql", dsn="mysql://user:password@localhost:3306/app", ) URL-style construction is also supported: pg, _ = fsspec.core.url_to_fs("db+postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/app") mysql, _ = fsspec.core.url_to_fs("db+mysql://user:password@localhost:3306/app") Both backends also accept individual connection options: pg = fsspec.filesystem( "db+postgresql", host="localhost", port=5432, database="app", user="user", password="password", sslmode="require", ) mysql = fsspec.filesystem( "db+mysql", host="localhost", port=3306, database="app", user="user", password="password", ssl_mode="REQUIRED", charset="utf8mb4", ) Pool sizing can be set for both networked backends with min_connections and max_connections: pg = fsspec.filesystem( "db+postgresql", dsn="postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/app", min_connections=1, max_c

t: How to read and write SQLite data
x: How to read and write SQLite data Install fsspec-db and connect to an existing database: python -m pip install fsspec-db import fsspec fs = fsspec.filesystem("db+sqlite", database="app.db") The examples below require a users table with name TEXT and score REAL columns. For a complete database setup, start with the tutorial. Inspect and read fs.ls("/", detail=False) fs.ls("/main", detail=False) fs.info("/main/users/columns/name") table = fs.query("SELECT name, score FROM users WHERE score > ?", [1.0]) Read a format-selecting path when the consumer needs a file: import pyarrow.ipc as ipc with fs.open("/main/users.arrow?limit=100", "rb") as file: table = ipc.open_stream(file).read_all() Append rows Encode rows as Arrow IPC and close the handle to commit: import pyarrow as pa import pyarrow.ipc as ipc rows = pa.table({"name": ["Ada"], "score": [1.0]}) sink = pa.BufferOutputStream() with ipc.new_stream(sink, rows.schema) as writer: writer.write_table(rows) with fs.open("/main/users.arrow", "ab") as file: file.write(sink.getvalue().to_pybytes()) Use "wb" only when replacing all existing rows.
